title: Past the Brewery
passage:
Ask anyone on the high street here where the swimming baths are, and you will be sent past the old brewery, left at the chemist, and on until the road bends at the bus station. The brewery has been eleven flats since 1998. The chemist moved to the retail park and the unit is a barber’s. Only the bus station is still a bus station. None of it is offered apologetically, and none of it slowly: the whole set arrives in one breath, and the person answering has moved off before the last turning is out of their mouth. Naming a shop that shut before the asker was born is second ___(1)___.

The practice gets read as carelessness, or as fondness for a town that no longer exists. The landmarks are not picked for visibility; they are the points at which the person speaking has turned for thirty years. The route therefore comes out in the right order while the names on it stay private. Directions built like this ___(2)___ badly. Passed to a second stranger, they keep their shape and lose their meaning. Almost every set ends with the same warning: if you reach the river, you have gone too far. That sentence asks nothing at all of whoever hears it.

The usual complaint is that the habit is sentimental. It is not. Nobody names the brewery fondly; anyone asked will tell you the beer was bad. The cost is duller and is paid one person at a time: twenty minutes, a wrong turning, and the same answer at the same corner, because the answer was never wrong. Admitting to not knowing would have cost nothing and saved the twenty minutes. Here, though, a shrug is heard as ___(3)___, and the town will take being wrong over being thought cold. ___(4)___, an answer is always produced, and it comes at the speed of a reflex.

A shopkeeper near the level crossing, asked for the baths four or five times a week, now comes out onto the pavement and points. It works, and nobody else has copied it. Most visitors take all this in their ___(5)___; a few go home with something to say about the place. The pointing arm goes back inside when the shop gets busy.
– Kester Orrenshaw, from a monthly column on English towns

questions.rationale: Collocation gap. All four options are common abstract nouns ending in -ture, so the set is POS-uniform and fully suffix-rhymed, and shape gives no purchase. The frame is 'Naming a shop that shut before the asker was born is second ___', and the fixed English collocation for an act performed without deliberation is 'second nature'. The sentence before it supplies the sense the idiom carries: the whole set of directions arrives in one breath and the speaker has already turned away, i.e. no thought was spent on it. 'nature' locks. fixture = collocation_misfit and the most thematic lure in the set: a vanished brewery that everyone still steers by is exactly what English calls a local fixture, so the word feels as though the passage has been reaching for it, but 'is second fixture' has no reading; without an article the noun cannot even take the ordinal, and with one it would mean the second match in a season. texture = collocation_misfit: right POS, right suffix, and vaguely available as a metaphor for the feel of a place, yet 'second texture' collocates with nothing. juncture = collocation_misfit: the noun is idiomatic only inside 'at this juncture', and without an article 'is second juncture' is not even grammatical, so the temptation is purely shape-based. Only 'nature' completes the idiom the frame demands.

Collocation gap. All four options are intransitive verbs of movement in the same bare form, agreeing with the plural 'Directions', so the set is POS-uniform and thematically matched to a passage about getting from one place to another - the shape and the topic both point at every option equally. The frame is 'Directions built like this ___ badly', and English has one verb that takes an adverb of quality to mean 'survives transfer to another context poorly': wine travels badly, a joke travels badly. The following sentence spells the mechanism out - passed to a second stranger, the directions keep their shape and lose their meaning - so the sense required is portability, and 'travel' locks. journey = collocation_misfit and the strongest lure, because 'journey' is the closest available synonym of 'travel' and the topic makes it feel apt; but as a verb 'journey' is intransitive in the literal sense only and never carries the figurative 'transfers well or badly' reading, so 'journey badly' has no idiomatic use. migrate = collocation_misfit: right POS, movement semantics, and a real verb of relocation, yet things do not migrate well or badly. commute = collocation_misfit: a movement verb tied to a daily route, which the passage is full of, but 'commute badly' says nothing about a set of directions. Only 'travel' takes this frame.

Polarity gap. All four options are abstract -ility nouns of similar length and register, so nothing separates them on shape. The frame is contrastive twice over: the sentence before it says that admitting ignorance 'would have cost nothing and saved the twenty minutes', and the gapped sentence opens 'Here, though', which reverses that accounting; the clause after the gap then states the price the town is willing to pay - 'the town will take being wrong over being thought cold'. Cold is the anchor: the gap must name what a refusal to answer is taken for, and it must sit at the negative pole. 'hostility' locks. civility = polarity_mirror and the designed trap: a shrug that withholds a bad answer reads to a skimmer as restraint or good manners, and 'civility' is the warm-pole social noun the earlier sentence about cost invites; but the frame demands the reading the town fears, and being thought civil is not something a town would trade accuracy to avoid. futility = surface_word_match: the paragraph has just totalled up twenty wasted minutes and a wrong turning, so the vocabulary of pointlessness is in the reader's ear, yet a silence is not heard 'as futility' by the person who asked, and futility names an outcome rather than a stance towards a stranger. docility = collocation and sense misfit: right suffix, right social-manner field, but a shrug is not an act of submissiveness and nothing in the paragraph supports it. Only 'hostility' satisfies both the reversal and the 'thought cold' anchor.

Connective gap. All four options are formal sentence-initial adverbs of the same class and the same Con- shape, so register and form separate nothing. The sentence before it establishes a social cost: a shrug is heard as hostility, and the town would rather be wrong than be thought cold. The gapped sentence reports what follows from that pressure - an answer is always produced, at the speed of a reflex. The relation is straightforwardly causal, and 'Consequently' locks. Conversely = wrong_logic: it demands that the second statement invert the first, and always producing an answer is not the inverse of fearing to be thought cold - it is its result. Concurrently = wrong_logic: it asserts that two things happen at the same time, but the gapped clause is a general truth about what the town always does, not an event running alongside another event. Conceivably = wrong_logic and the deliberate hedge trap: it frames the clause as a possibility the writer is entertaining, which collides with the flat 'always' inside the sentence it introduces and with the reportorial certainty of the whole paragraph. Note for the hedge audit: here the key is the confident, unqualified connective and the cautious-sounding option is the wrong one, so the test-wise habit of choosing the moderate option scores zero on this gap.

Collocation gap. All four options are short concrete nouns from the vocabulary of walking, which is exactly the field the passage has been working in, so every option is thematically flattering and none is separable on shape or register. The frame is 'Most visitors take all this in their ___', and the fixed English idiom for absorbing a setback without complaint is 'take it in one's stride'. The clause after the semicolon confirms the sense by naming the minority who do not absorb it and go home with something to say. 'stride' locks. step = collocation_misfit and the sharpest trap in the unit: 'in step' is a real English phrase and the possessive frame looks close enough that a solver who half-remembers the idiom will take it, but 'take it in their step' is not English. pace = collocation_misfit: 'at their own pace' exists and is about walking speed, which is the passage's own subject matter, yet nothing is ever taken in a person's pace. gait = collocation_misfit: a real, precise noun for a manner of walking, maximally on-theme after four paragraphs of directions, and it collocates with nothing at all in this frame. Only 'stride' completes the idiom.
